notice: Generic, anonymized templates distilled from past fractional and consulting proposals. Contains no client names, people, identifying figures or verbatim client text. Example sentences are illustrative and newly written. {{field}} placeholders are filled from discovery, the rate index, or the user.

fieldSources.discovery: Extracted from a discovery-call transcript or notes and confirmed by the user before use
fieldSources.rate_index: Suggested by the Merlin rate index by company stage, seat and hours
fieldSources.profile: From the fractional's own Merlin profile

blocks.title: Cover
blocks.purpose: Lead with the outcome, not the service, and show who it is for.
blocks.guidance: Headline states the result in plain words. Include 'prepared for' (name and title of the signer), 'prepared by', date, and version. One subtitle sentence on the shape of the engagement.
goodLooksLike: Addressed to the person who signs
commonMistakes: Headline is the service name only
Addressed to a go-between instead of the signer
exampleText: Build the sales system first, then hire into it.
A senior operator embedded two days a week to take you from a flat year to a repeatable plan.

blocks.title: What we heard
blocks.purpose: Prove you listened before you prescribe, in the buyer's own vocabulary.
blocks.guidance: 4 to 6 headed bullets. Each is one pain with one concrete fact (a rate, a duration, a count). Reference the date of the call. Paraphrase; never paste transcript text. Soften personnel issues; the document will be forwarded.
goodLooksLike: Ordered from most to least painful
commonMistakes: Generic statements any company could receive
Naming or criticizing individual employees bluntly
exampleText: Your sales seat has been empty for three weeks, and the CRM it relied on was set up for a different business line.
Conversion on qualified calls has fallen sharply since the price change, and the cycle now runs several weeks longer.

fields.label: One paraphrased line in the buyer's voice (optional, confirm with buyer)

blocks.title: The moment
blocks.purpose: Create urgency from the buyer's own trigger event and the cost of waiting.
blocks.guidance: 2 to 4 lines or 3 to 4 stat callouts: the trigger (seat empty, new leader, competitor exit, board target), the gap to the goal, and what a quarter of delay costs.
goodLooksLike: Cost of inaction stated in the buyer's terms
exampleText: An empty seat is the cheapest moment to build the system the next hire will run.
A competitor stepping back opens a window that will not stay open past next year's budget cycle.

blocks.title: Diagnosis
blocks.purpose: Reframe the problem so the recommended shape follows naturally.
blocks.guidance: Open with a one-line reframe ('This isn't X, it's Y'). Follow with 3 to 5 numbered patterns you have seen before. Each pattern should point to a workstream.
commonMistakes: Diagnosis that does not lead to the recommendation
exampleText: This isn't a hiring problem. It's a missing system that no hire could invent while also carrying a quota.
Every inquiry gets the same treatment today, so the best-fit buyers wait behind broad RFPs.

blocks.title: The math
blocks.purpose: Tie the engagement to the buyer's own target and show the gap honestly.
blocks.guidance: Work backward: goal, deals needed, opportunities, meetings, activity, using stated assumptions. Mark which assumptions Workstream 1 will validate. State an honest first-quarter goal. Do not promise the target.
exampleText: At your average first-year contract value, the growth goal needs roughly ten new clients a month after churn; today's pace is about three.
Restoring last year's conversion rate on the same lead volume would close about half of that gap before any new channel is added.

blocks.title: What we recommend
blocks.purpose: State the engagement shape: seat(s), seniority, commitment, mandate, and what it is not.
blocks.guidance: Title, days per week or hours per month, one-sentence mandate, and an explicit 'This is not a ___ role.' For two seats, show each as a card with responsibilities and allocation.
commonMistakes: Multiple options when none were requested
exampleText: A VP-level operator, two days a week, who owns the revenue plan and the operating rhythm so the founder gets her week back.
This is not a sales manager seat. Your director keeps running the day to day and gains a strategist above her.

blocks.title: Role profile and selection
blocks.purpose: Show you know what good looks like and set up the shortlist.
blocks.guidance: Must-haves tied to stage and motion; nice-to-haves tied to industry; explicit 'not a fit'. Explain selection: number of profiles, buyer meets as many as they like, optional 'walk us through your first month' exercise.
commonMistakes: Naming a person before availability is confirmed
exampleText: Has personally closed new business at a company under five million in revenue, not only managed the people who did.
Not a fit: a leader who expects a team, systems and leads to already be in place.

blocks.title: Plan: phases and workstreams
blocks.purpose: Make the work concrete, sequenced and checkable.
blocks.guidance: 2 to 3 phases. Inside, 3 to 7 workstreams, each with a week range, 3 to 6 approach bullets, a Deliverable line and an Expected impact line. Optionally mark 'Start now' vs 'Can wait' with what waiting costs. Prefer deliverables over hours.
goodLooksLike: Every workstream has a named deliverable
Expected impact stated as direction, not a guarantee
exampleText: Deliverable: a one-page sales process with named stages, required activities and a black-and-white exit gate for every stage.
Expected impact: the next sales hire starts on a working system instead of spending their first quarter building one.

fields.label: Workstreams (title, weeks, approach[], deliverable, expectedImpact, priority)

blocks.title: Milestones
blocks.purpose: Give the buyer decision points, not just status updates.
blocks.guidance: Day 30 / 60 / 90 (or dates). Each milestone ends with a decision for the buyer.
goodLooksLike: Each milestone ends in a decision
Includes the renewal or scale decision
exampleText: Day 30: diagnostic readout with a ranked list of changes. You choose what we fix first.
Day 90: plan and team assessment presented; decide to continue, scale up, or wrap.

blocks.title: Success measures
blocks.purpose: Define what the buyer can point to by day 90.
blocks.guidance: 3 to 6 measurable leading indicators. Baselines set at day 30. Avoid committing to revenue outcomes not controllable in 90 days.
exampleText: A live view of every open opportunity, reviewed weekly by the team that owns it.
A response-time baseline for new inquiries, with a target agreed at the day 30 readout.

blocks.title: Operating cadence
blocks.purpose: Show what a normal week looks like after the build phase.
blocks.guidance: Table or 5 to 8 lines: pipeline review, 1:1s, forecast memo, leadership sync, written weekly update. Optional hour split per day.
goodLooksLike: Written weekly update to the sponsor
exampleText: Every Monday you receive a short written forecast: pacing, what changed, and the plan for anything off track.

blocks.title: Reporting structure
blocks.purpose: Settle who reports to whom and who decides.
blocks.guidance: Fractional reports to ___; who reports to the fractional; client decides on hires, exits, pricing; fractional recommends. Note the provider remains accountable for delivery and replacement.
commonMistakes: Fractional implied to make personnel decisions
exampleText: Decisions on hiring, exits and pricing stay with you. We bring the analysis and a written recommendation.

blocks.title: Assumptions and client responsibilities
blocks.purpose: Make the client a co-owner of pace and protect scope.
blocks.guidance: Data and system access in week one; standing weekly sponsor session; stakeholder availability; team-size cap the price assumes; tools paid by client.
commonMistakes: No dependencies, so delays become the fractional's fault
exampleText: A standing 30-minute weekly session with you is the single biggest factor in how fast this gets built, because the process we are documenting is yours.
This scope is priced for a team of up to five; a larger team is handled by written amendment.

blocks.title: Out of scope
blocks.purpose: Prevent scope creep by naming what a buyer might assume is included.
blocks.guidance: 3 to 6 items, each 'available by written amendment'. Common: closing deals personally, recruiting, CRM administration, marketing execution, system integrations.
goodLooksLike: Specific to this buyer's likely assumptions
commonMistakes: So long it reads as defensive
exampleText: Recruiting or placing additional sales headcount. We can add this by written amendment.

blocks.title: Why fractional
blocks.purpose: Support the decision against a full-time hire or a consulting firm.
blocks.guidance: Comparison table: time to seat, time to impact, fully loaded annual cost (ranges), exit cost if wrong, signal to the team. Use as support, not the centerpiece.
goodLooksLike: Includes the 'if the call is wrong' row
exampleText: A full-time search takes a quarter to seat and another two to show impact; an embedded operator is producing artifacts in the first month.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.purpose: Earn credibility with the closest analog, not the biggest logo.
blocks.guidance: About (3 lines), how operators are vetted and matched (required variables plus one strong preference), and 1 to 2 case studies with the same problem shape as the buyer's. Anonymize unless the reference has consented.
goodLooksLike: Matching criteria specific to this brief
commonMistakes: Case study from a different motion or stage
exampleText: A founder-led platform selling to a technical buyer who ignores generic outreach. Sound familiar?

blocks.title: Team and rates
blocks.purpose: Show who does what on multi-role engagements.
blocks.guidance: Table of role, function, responsibilities, estimated hours or share. If packaged as flat fees, say so and show standard overage rates.
commonMistakes: Too many roles for the size of the work
exampleText: One lead owns every deliverable; specialists from the bench join for specific workstreams.

blocks.title: Timeline and investment
blocks.purpose: State the commercial terms clearly in one place.
blocks.guidance: Initial term and what follows; monthly fee with hours/days or 'priced on deliverables'; step-down from month 4 if applicable; variable compensation basis (collected revenue, window); overage rate with written consent; billing in advance and due date; late fee and work-pause rule; replacement guarantee; conversion fee.
goodLooksLike: One price for the recommended option
commonMistakes: Deferring price to a later email
Variable pay on booked rather than collected revenue
exampleText: The first three months are the build and carry the heavier allocation; from month four the engagement continues month to month at a lower steady-state fee.
If the selected operator is not the right fit at any point, we present replacements and transition the work at no added cost.

fields.label: Hours per month or days per week
Written consent required above (% of allocation)
Full-time conversion fee (flat or % of salary, tail days)

blocks.title: Payment schedule
blocks.purpose: Remove ambiguity on when money moves.
blocks.guidance: Table of invoice number, date, amount, period covered. Pro-rate partial first periods.
commonMistakes: Schedule that contradicts the investment block
exampleText: Invoice 1 covers the partial first period and is due on signing; later invoices follow on the same day each month.

blocks.title: Potential next phases
blocks.purpose: Plant the expansion path without inflating today's scope.
blocks.guidance: 3 to 5 bullets of logical follow-on work, each one line, explicitly not included in this agreement.
commonMistakes: Smuggling future work into current price
exampleText: Packaging the expansion services into named, priced offers once the pilot shows which accounts buy.

blocks.title: Next steps
blocks.purpose: Close with a dated path and a commitment.
blocks.guidance: Dated table (when, what, owner), starting with the completed discovery call and ending with the operator starting. Add a one-line commitment. Book the next meeting before sending.
goodLooksLike: Every row dated with an owner
exampleText: If you select us, you will have a named shortlist within five business days and an operator in seat within three weeks.

blocks.title: Terms and conditions
blocks.purpose: Standard consulting agreement the SOW attaches to.
blocks.guidance: Library clause set with variables: services; payments and expenses; independent contractor; confidentiality (survival years); non-solicitation (months); work product and background IP license; term and termination; subcontracting with named operator acknowledged; indemnification; injunctive relief; governing law and arbitration; entire agreement; conversion fee; notices; severability and misclassification savings; counterparts and electronic signature; survival; counsel acknowledgment. Have counsel approve the library; users change variables, not clause text.
commonMistakes: Inconsistent conversion fee between SOW and terms

blocks.title: Consulting agreement
blocks.purpose: The agreement itself, in plain words and numbered, so the client can open any part and read it in full before signing.
blocks.guidance: One numbered part per clause, each a short title then its text: services, fees and payment, independent contractor, confidential information, work product, term and ending it, general. Keep the clause text your counsel approved and change only the names, numbers and dates. The client reads each part as a line they can open, the first one open.
goodLooksLike: Numbered parts, each with a title of a few words
The same notice and term as the investment section
commonMistakes: One long paragraph the client cannot scan
A notice period that differs from the investment section

fields.label: Confidential information is kept private for (years after the work ends)

blocks.title: Signature
blocks.purpose: Electronic signature by both parties.
blocks.guidance: Client signer and provider signer, each with name, title and date captured by the e-sign flow. Track viewed and signed events; countersign; store executed PDF with audit trail; on client signature, trigger the operator subcontract.
commonMistakes: Signer is not the economic buyer

blocks.title: Addendum reference
blocks.purpose: Extend an existing agreement without renegotiating terms.
blocks.guidance: One paragraph: references the original agreement and date, states that its terms continue, and lists only what changes (hours, seat, term, rate). Follow with the invoice schedule and signatures.
exampleText: This addendum follows the terms of our original agreement and changes only the monthly allocation and the term below.

templates.title: Fractional sales leader: build, then lead
templates.bestFor: Founder-led or plateaued companies roughly $2-20M in revenue that need a sales leader to build process and run the team, or a builder who sells.
templates.pricingGuidance: Heavier allocation months 1-3 (build), step-down from month 4. Broad bands: about $4-6K/mo for ~20 hrs with a small team; about $5-15K/mo for 20-40 hrs or 1-2 days/week at $5-20M. For a builder who sells, consider fixed plus a share of collected revenue on new contracts. Initial term 3-4 months, then month to month with 30 days' notice; optional day-90 opt-out.

exampleText: A fractional VP of Sales who owns the plan and holds the team to it, while your director keeps running the daily motion.

overrides.guidance: Phase 1 (days 1-90): benchmark the current state, build the process with stage gates, script the customer moments, train and coach, assess the team. Phase 2 (day 91+): run the weekly meeting, 1:1s, call review, forecast, written weekly update.

templates.title: 90-day program with an embedded lead
templates.bestFor: PE-backed or larger companies ($20M+) needing a foundation or transformation build with one accountable lead positioned inside the leadership team.
templates.pricingGuidance: Flat monthly program fee priced on deliverables, not hours; firm initial term of 90 days to 6 months, then month to month. Broad band about $15-30K/mo. If a sponsor signals a cap, present 2-3 intensity options with scope for each rather than discounting.

exampleText: The program is delivered by an embedded team under one accountable lead who sits with your leadership, not as an outside advisory engagement.

overrides.guidance: Phase 1 embed and diagnose (days 1-30) ending in a ranked backlog; Phase 2 confirm then execute in short increments. 5-7 workstreams marked Start now / Can wait with deliverable and expected impact each. Agree month-4 priorities in writing by day 45.
Include at least one case study from the buyer's industry or an equivalent problem shape; sponsors ask for it explicitly.

templates.title: Ongoing retainer or expansion addendum
templates.bestFor: Existing clients: continuing after a build phase, adding hours or a second seat, or extending the term.
templates.pricingGuidance: Keep the original rate unless the scope or seniority changes; state the new allocation, effective date, re-evaluation date and invoice schedule. Month to month with 30 days' notice after any committed period.

overrides.guidance: Only if responsibilities change: list the updated responsibilities as short headed bullets.

templates.title: RevOps or systems build project
templates.bestFor: Defined builds: CRM migration or rebuild, sales playbook, outbound engine, lead scoring, AI-assisted workflow.
templates.pricingGuidance: Fixed fee by phase over 6-12 weeks (broadly about $5-35K total), billed on signing then by month or phase; optional ongoing optimization retainer afterward (broadly about $5-6K/mo). Deliverable acceptance window and change orders above a set threshold.

overrides.guidance: Typical: Phase 1 discovery and audit (weeks 1-2); Phase 2 build or playbook (weeks 3-6); Phase 3 configuration and tooling (weeks 5-8); Phase 4 enablement and rollout (weeks 7-10). Each phase lists approach and deliverables. State what is a recommendation only vs implemented.

templates.title: Advisory engagement
templates.bestFor: Pre-seed to early-stage founders, or an investor or operator supporting a small portfolio, who need foundational go-to-market guidance at low intensity.
templates.pricingGuidance: Half a day to one day per week; broad band about $2-5K/mo; month to month. Buyers at this stage want a clear number up front.

exampleText: Half a day a week focused on three foundations: who you sell to, how you reach them, and a simple pipeline you can run yourself.

discoveryExtraction.description: Fields to extract from a discovery-call transcript to pre-fill a proposal. Extracted values are paraphrased and shown to the user for confirmation; never paste transcript text into a client document.

fields.extract: Industry, model, revenue band, headcount, ownership, regions
Revenue or customer target with deadline
What good looks like at 90 days and 12 months
Roles, tenure, performers, incumbents to protect
Deal flow, number of meetings, handoffs
CRM, tools, data sources, adoption
4-6 pains with one fact each
Conversion, cycle length, win rate, deal value, lead volume, spend
Failed hires, agencies, tools and why
Trigger event and cost of waiting
Desired start, blackout dates, decision date
Signer, reviewers, committee, competing vendors
Was the economic buyer on the call (boolean)
Caps, market quotes, sensitivity, preferred structure
Seat, seniority, days/week, builder/manager/closer
Must-have, nice-to-have, not-a-fit
Sponsor, champion, users, incumbents (stored privately)
Data access, sponsor time, references
Personnel issues, words to avoid, confidentiality
Work the client handles or doesn't want
Concerns raised
Agreed follow-up date and owner

riskFlags.message: The person who signs was not on the call. Proposals routed through a go-between lost more often; ask to present to the signer.
No budget signal captured. Ask for a range or market quotes before sending to avoid sticker shock.
No dated next step. Book the review meeting before sending.
Present at least two profiles; a single candidate gives the buyer no choice.

riskFlags.when: pricing.monthlyFee is empty and pricing.model != fixed_fee_phased
riskFlags.message: State a price. Deferring it to a later email stalled deals.
Above the typical band for this stage. Consider 2-3 intensity options.

objectionLibrary.response: Offer 2-3 intensity levels with scope for each; tie back to the math; reduce scope rather than rate; show the step-down after the build phase.
Too early to know who to hire before the leaks are diagnosed; a full-time search takes months to seat; build the system first and hire into it, with a defined conversion path.
Named operator, vetted bench, one contract and invoice, replacement guarantee, provider accountable for delivery.
One embedded accountable lead inside the leadership team, a live backlog and a monthly deliverables summary.
Leading-indicator milestones at days 30/60/90, an explicit opt-out, and for first hires a fixed ramp then performance pay.
Build before hire; past hires struggled because they had to invent the system while closing.

objectionLibrary.objection: Need the CEO, owner or board
objectionLibrary.response: Offer to join that meeting, send a one-page summary, and book the date before ending the call.
Show the closest same-shape analog and the matching criteria you will screen for.
Agencies need a proven internal process to work from; document it first, then outsource execution against it.
